reviewMethod: Independent visual inspection of all eight original paper pages and scheme pages 39–82, including every optional question, published allocation, restricted award, original diagram and alternative method. All 57 question and 57 complete solution presentations inspected.
sourceNotes: Whole-examination choice of five Section A questions and one Section B question does not remove any of the eleven offered questions from practice. All are retained.
Q7(b): one novel, one play and one poem are random scenario outcomes, not a finite candidate answer menu. Each requested probability is one task.
Q9(b): one correct answer out of four defines the probability model, not a candidate selection pool. Four, five or six correct in part (iii) is the union of three required events.
Q11(c)(i): transformation to/from the unit circle or another method are alternative proof methods for the same marked task.

Q10(b)(v) asks the candidate to construct an isomorphism. No finite pool of candidate maps is printed; the six listed permutations define the group. Retain one construction task, with complete alternative proofs.

Both roots, both intercepts, all required angles, all order-two subgroups, and the complete order-three subgroup are required responses, not optional routes. Password strings are illustrative examples. No finite printed choose pool requires expansion.
Mathematical errors or omissions: −3. Numerical slips: −1. Misreadings: −1 provided the task is not oversimplified.
A correct relevant step earns its attempt mark; deductions cannot reduce it below that floor. No mark strictly between zero and the attempt mark.
Worthless work: zero. Hit or miss: full marks or zero.
Best of two or more attempts accepted unless indicated otherwise; same error in same section penalised once.
Particular cases, unrequested verifications/diagrams, and serious blunders/omissions/misreadings earn attempt marks at most.
Detailed task-specific exceptions and caps must remain beside all official worked alternatives.

Every independently marked printed part is retained. Named scoring steps within one proof or calculation remain components of that task; alternative solution methods do not multiply question counts or tariffs.
Independent visual sweep: all eight paper PDF pages and all scheme pages 39–82, including every Section B option and complete general and special marking notes.
57 tasks across eleven questions: 4, 6, 5, 5, 5, 3, 6, 6, 5, 7, 5. Each question offers 50 marks: 550 offered against the 300-mark examination selection.

The two printed radius calculations contain √(16 + 2). This should be √(16 + 4) = √20. The final circle (x − 6)² + (y − 2)² = 20 is correct. The mediator line should read 3y − 3 = x − 3, hence x − 3y = 0; the next simultaneous equations use this correct relation.
The worked answer changes the label to PQR in its last line. The angle requested and calculated is QPR, at P: 30° or 150°.
The paper allows any real a. The printed standard deviations omit the absolute value: the correct results are √2 |a| in (i) and 3√2 |a| in (ii). The scheme’s expressions are correct only when a ≥ 0.
The paper allows any real a. The printed standard deviations omit the absolute value: the correct results are √2 |a| in (i) and 3√2 |a| in (ii). The scheme’s expressions are correct only when a ≥ 0.
The slip note says two decimal places, but the paper and model answer require three. Use three decimal places.
The exact interval is 80 ± 1.96(6/√50) grams, approximately [78.3369, 81.6631]. To one decimal place this is [78.3, 81.7], not the printed [78.3, 81.6].

The paper prints ℝ ∖ {−1}. For the intended group and inverse rule, the domain should be ℝ ∖ {1}: 1 has no inverse, and the printed domain is not closed under the operation. The identity is 0; for x ≠ 1 the inverse is x/(x − 1).

The paper prints ℝ ∖ {−1}. For the intended group and inverse rule, the domain should be ℝ ∖ {1}: 1 has no inverse, and the printed domain is not closed under the operation. The identity is 0; for x ≠ 1 the inverse is x/(x − 1).
The model assumes that the major axis lies along the x-axis. The question does not state its orientation; rotated ellipses with the same axes also meet the stated conditions.
The source page mislabels this task as (c)(i) and 11(b)(ii); it is Q11(b)(i). Both the geometric and coordinate proofs below address the requested midpoint result.
The first displayed transformation prints y′ = y/10. It should be y′ = y/5, consistent with the subsequent inverse transformation and image coordinates.

cards.questionText: Find the equation of the circle with centre (3, −4) passing through (7, −3).
Find the centre and radius of the circle.
cards.stem: The circle has equation x² + y² − 8x − 10y + 32 = 0.

cards.questionText: The line 3x + 4y + k = 0 is tangent to the circle. Find the two possible values of k.
cards.stem: The circle has equation x² + y² − 8x − 10y + 32 = 0.
cards.markingNote: Accept the candidate’s centre and radius from part (b)(i). Both values of k are required.

cards.questionText: Find the equation of a circle that has y = 2x as a tangent at (2, 4) and also passes through (4, −2).
cards.markingNote: The 15-mark finish allows only 0, 5 or 15: the scheme explicitly permits no slips or blunders in this component.

cards.questionText: Express the position vector c in terms of i and j.
cards.stem: A, B and C are points and O is the origin. a = 2i + 3j, b = −3i − 6j, and vector AC = vector OB.

cards.questionText: Express |v| and u · v in terms of k.
cards.stem: u = 2i + j and v = −i + kj, where k is real.

cards.questionText: Given cos θ = −1/√2, where θ is the angle between u and v, find the two possible values of k.
cards.stem: u = 2i + j and v = −i + kj, where k is real.

cards.questionText: Express q in terms of a and c.
cards.stem: OABC is a parallelogram with O as origin. Q is the midpoint of BC. AQ is extended to R so that QR = AQ. Lower-case letters denote position vectors.

cards.questionText: Express vector AQ in terms of a and c.
cards.stem: OABC is a parallelogram with O as origin. Q is the midpoint of BC. AQ is extended to R so that QR = AQ. Lower-case letters denote position vectors.

cards.questionText: Show that O, C and R are collinear.
cards.stem: OABC is a parallelogram with O as origin. Q is the midpoint of BC. AQ is extended to R so that QR = AQ. Lower-case letters denote position vectors.

cards.questionText: The line 3x + 4y − 7 = 0 is perpendicular to ax − 6y − 1 = 0. Find a.
Write down the coordinates of P and Q in terms of k.
cards.stem: The line 4x − 5y + k = 0 meets the x-axis at P and the y-axis at Q; O is the origin.

cards.questionText: The area of triangle OPQ is 10 square units. Find the two possible values of k.
cards.stem: The line 4x − 5y + k = 0 meets the x-axis at P and the y-axis at Q; O is the origin.

cards.questionText: Find the equation of f(l), the image of l under f.
cards.stem: The transformation f maps (x, y) to (x′, y′), where x′ = x + y and y′ = x − y. The line l has equation y = mx + c.

cards.questionText: Find every value of m for which f(l) makes an angle of 45° with l.
cards.stem: The transformation f maps (x, y) to (x′, y′), where x′ = x + y and y′ = x − y. The line l has equation y = mx + c.
cards.markingNote: All three solutions m = 0, 1 and −1 are required; otherwise the award is at most the attempt mark 6. At m = −1 the image is vertical and still satisfies the condition.

cards.questionText: Triangle PQR has area 20 cm², PQ = 10 cm and PR = 8 cm. Find the two possible values of angle QPR.
Find all solutions of cos 2x = cos x for 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°.
Show that the area of triangle ABC is ½r(a + b + c).
cards.stem: Triangle ABC has sides a, b and c and an incircle of centre O and radius r, as shown.

cards.questionText: Show that this triangle is right-angled.
cards.stem: Triangle ABC has sides a, b and c and an incircle of centre O and radius r, as shown. The side lengths are a = p² + q², b = p² − q² and c = 2pq, where p and q are natural numbers with p > q.

cards.questionText: Show that the radius of the incircle is a whole number.
cards.stem: Triangle ABC has sides a, b and c and an incircle of centre O and radius r, as shown. The side lengths are a = p² + q², b = p² − q² and c = 2pq, where p and q are natural numbers with p > q. You may use the area identity ½r(a + b + c) and the right-angle result from the preceding parts.

cards.questionText: Given tan θ = 1/3, show that tan 2θ = 3/4.
cards.markingNote: The alternative triangle method must account for both the first and third quadrants.

cards.questionText: Using the cosine rule, show that cos A + cos C = 7/8.
cards.stem: The triangle has sides 4, 5 and 6, with angles A, B and C labelled in the original diagram.

cards.questionText: Show that cos(A + C) = −9/16.
cards.stem: The triangle has sides 4, 5 and 6, with angles A, B and C labelled in the original diagram.

cards.questionText: Prove the stated trigonometric identity.
cards.stem: (cos A + cos B)² + (sin A + sin B)² = 2 + 2 cos(A − B).

cards.questionText: Hence solve (cos 4x + cos x)² + (sin 4x + sin x)² = 2 + 2√3 sin 3x for 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°.
cards.stem: Use the identity (cos A + cos B)² + (sin A + sin B)² = 2 + 2 cos(A − B).
cards.markingNote: For the 10-mark solutions component: all six values earn 10, exactly one omitted or incorrect value earns 3, and more than one omitted or incorrect value earns 0.

cards.questionText: One bag has four red and six blue discs; another has five red and seven yellow discs. One disc is drawn from each. What is the probability both are red?
Prove that p uₙ₊₂ + q uₙ₊₁ + r uₙ = 0 for all natural n.
cards.stem: α and β are the roots of px² + qx + r = 0. The sequence is uₙ = lαⁿ + mβⁿ for all natural n.

cards.questionText: Six people sit at random in a row of 11 seats. How much more likely is it that all six sit together than that no two sit together?
cards.markingNote: Only 0, 6, 17 or 20 are permitted. The exceptional 17 is for both probabilities correct but subtracted rather than divided; otherwise the published awards are 0, 6 or 20.

cards.questionText: Show that there are more than a million permitted passwords.
cards.stem: A password has four characters chosen from capital letters A–Z and digits 0–9, and starts with a letter. BA7A, C999 and DGKK are allowed; 7DCA is not.

cards.questionText: Find the probability Karen has studied all three of the texts on the exam.
cards.stem: Karen’s English course has six novels, four plays and ten poems. The exam asks about one text of each type. She has studied four novels, three plays and seven poems.

cards.questionText: Find the probability Karen has studied none of the texts on the exam.
cards.stem: Karen’s English course has six novels, four plays and ten poems. The exam asks about one text of each type. She has studied four novels, three plays and seven poems.

cards.questionText: Find the probability Karen has studied at least two of the texts on the exam.
cards.stem: Karen’s English course has six novels, four plays and ten poems. The exam asks about one text of each type. She has studied four novels, three plays and seven poems.

cards.questionText: Express μ and σ in terms of a.
cards.stem: The real numbers a, 2a, 3a, 4a and 5a have mean μ and standard deviation σ.

cards.questionText: Hence write down the mean and standard deviation of 3a + 5, 6a + 5, 9a + 5, 12a + 5 and 15a + 5.
cards.stem: The real numbers a, 2a, 3a, 4a and 5a have mean μ and standard deviation σ.

cards.questionText: Write an expression for the area of the rectangle in terms of p.
cards.stem: A rectangle is inscribed between y = 9 − x² and the x-axis as shown; p is its positive half-width.

cards.questionText: Hence calculate the area of the largest possible rectangle.
cards.stem: A rectangle is inscribed between y = 9 − x² and the x-axis as shown; p is its positive half-width. First write the area in terms of p.
cards.markingNote: The source explicitly awards 0 for this part if part (b)(i) earns 0. The area-expression prompt and diagram remain attached.

cards.questionText: Derive the Maclaurin series for f(x) = cos x up to and including the x⁶ term.
cards.markingNote: The expansion must be derived. Quoting the correct expansion without derivation earns the attempt mark only.

cards.questionText: Hence, using sin²x = ½(1 − cos 2x), show the first three non-zero Maclaurin terms for sin²x are x² − x⁴/3 + 2x⁶/45.
cards.stem: Use the Maclaurin expansion of cos x derived in part (i).

cards.questionText: Use these terms to approximate sin²(½), as a fraction.
cards.stem: The first three non-zero terms of sin²x are x² − x⁴/3 + 2x⁶/45.

cards.questionText: Find the probability Seán gets exactly five answers correct. Give the answer to three decimal places.
cards.stem: A test has 20 multiple-choice questions, each with four possible answers and exactly one correct answer. Seán guesses every answer at random.

cards.questionText: Find the probability Seán gets four, five or six answers correct. Give the answer to three decimal places.
cards.stem: A test has 20 multiple-choice questions, each with four possible answers and exactly one correct answer. Seán guesses every answer at random.
cards.markingNote: Add the probabilities of four, five and six correct; retain precision until the final rounding.

cards.questionText: Form a 95% confidence interval for the mean weight of muffins produced by the bakery.
cards.stem: A random sample of 50 muffins has mean weight 80 grams and standard deviation 6 grams.

cards.stem: The operation is x ∗ y = x + y − xy. See the original printed domain and the source correction attached to the answer.

cards.stem: G is the group of the six permutations of {1, 2, 3} labelled a, b, c, d, f and g in the original table. The operation is composition.

cards.questionText: Give an isomorphism from K under composition to H under multiplication, fully justifying that it is an isomorphism.
cards.stem: G is the group of the six permutations of {1, 2, 3} labelled a, b, c, d, f and g in the original table. The operation is composition. K is the subgroup of order 3. H = {1, w, w²} is a group under multiplication, where w³ = 1.
cards.markingNote: A complete isomorphism needs an explicit map and full justification. All nine products or the published cyclic-group argument are accepted.
